title: The Answer to the King
sum: King Zedekiah, with Babylon's army camped outside Jerusalem, sends two men to ask Jeremiah for a miracle like the one that saved the city from Assyria in 701 BC (21:1-2). Jeremiah sends back the opposite. The LORD himself will turn the city's weapons around and fight against it "with a hand stretched out and a strong arm" (21:4-5), the very power that freed Israel from Egypt. The people may still choose: stay and die, or go out to the Chaldeans and live (21:8-9).

The chapter closes with a short call to David's house to do justice "each morning," and a threat of fire to the proud city on its rock (21:11-14). Chapters 21 to 23 together form a collection about the kings, which now begins with the last of them.
readings: Read as the city's last offer

Jeremiah's "way of life" is a real choice. The siege is not yet over, and the message to the people (21:8-10) lets them save their lives by leaving. His enemies called it treason (38:2-4); he called it the LORD's word, and the book remembers the people who survived by it.
Read as a judgment already decided

Another way hears the answer to Zedekiah (21:3-7) as sealed: the LORD has set his face against the city (21:10) and the king will be handed over. The offer to the people stands beside it, but the king and the city are beyond rescue. Both readings fit the text; the difference is whether the offer reaches the king.

views.H: The embassy comes early in the siege, about January 588 BC (52:4). Zedekiah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar in 597, has broken his oath of loyalty (Ezekiel 17:13-18) and hopes for a repeat of Hezekiah's escape. The Egyptian army that briefly draws Babylon away (37:5) may be a later stage of the same war. The city fell in the summer of 586 BC.
views.C: Much of the prose here (21:3-10) is written in the style Deuteronomy and Kings share, and scholars such as Thiel and Nicholson see the hand of a Deuteronomistic editor working over a core of Jeremiah's words. Others (Bright, Holladay) trace most of it to Jeremiah himself or to Baruch. The Greek is shorter at several points and differs in the list of calamities. The oracle in 21:11-14 is poetry and is probably older and separate; its placement here is editorial.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers Jeremiah as the faithful prophet who would not flatter the king, and Jeremiah 1-2 are among the readings of rebuke in the weeks of mourning before the Ninth of Av. The surrender advice is best understood as the LORD's decree about this siege, not a general rule for Israel's relation to empires.
views.X: Christian readers have taken Jeremiah's "way of life and way of death" as a pattern for the choice Jesus sets before people (Matthew 7:13-14), and it opens the Didache.
views.F: Futurist readers find little here beyond the historical siege; a few take the fire against the "forest" (21:14) as a pattern for later judgment on Jerusalem.

deep.h: Treason or word of the LORD?
deep.b:
On the usual reading Jeremiah's advice to leave the city and surrender is what made him an enemy of the royal court (38:2-6). A Judean army letter from Lachish, from the same war, says that the words of "the officials" "weaken the hands" of the people. It does not name Jeremiah, but the phrase is the one the officials use against him (38:4). The book's answer is that he spoke what the LORD said, and that the same word that condemned the king's policy saved the lives of those who listened. The book makes the point by contrast: Zedekiah's request is for a wonder; Jeremiah's reply is a choice.

Jeremiah's counsel is also not pacifism or a general rule about foreign rulers. It rests on the LORD's own decision (21:10) and on the fact that Nebuchadnezzar is in this war the LORD's servant (25:9; 27:6). The same prophet promises Babylon's fall when its time comes (25:12).

The Plain follows the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex). Where this part says "the Greek," it means Swete's printed text of Codex Vaticanus, not the critical text of Ziegler, which may differ in details. The Dead Sea scrolls are cited from the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (ETCBC dss), and only for words that are not restored. 4QJer-a (4Q70) has parts of 21:1 and of 22:3-16. 4QJer-c (4Q72) has parts of 21:7-10, 22:4-28, 24:6-7, 25:7-8, 25:15-17 and 25:24-26, many of its words restored. No scroll preserves any part of chapter 23. The Targum of Jeremiah (Hayward's translation), Rashi and Radak are named only where a note says what they read. The Vulgate and the Peshitta were not consulted.

echoes: Exodus 3:20; Deuteronomy 5:15; Deuteronomy 30:15-19; 2 Kings 19:1-7; Isaiah 37:36; Didache 1:1; Matthew 7:13-14; Ezekiel 17:13-18

settings.by: Jeremiah, speaking what he says is the LORD's word
settings.to: The king's two envoys, Pashhur son of Malkijah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, for Zedekiah; and in 21:8-10 for the people crowded inside Jerusalem
settings.when: Early in the Babylonian siege, about January 588 BC, with Nebuchadnezzar's army camped outside the walls
settings.why: Zedekiah wanted a wonder to drive Nebuchadnezzar away. Jeremiah answers that the LORD is on the other side and that the weapons of Judah's own defenders will fail. To the people he gives what the king would not: a choice, which is to leave and live or stay and die. Knowing the audience changes the meaning: this is a message to a besieged city, not a rule for all times.
settings.readers: Exiles reading the book after 586 would find in the chapter the reason for the fall: the king asked for help and was told to look at his own people's wrongs. It also showed them that the survivors of the siege lived because they listened.
views: Some commentators identify this with the embassy of 37:3-10, when an Egyptian army had drawn the Babylonians off. Most see them as two requests at different stages of the siege, since Zedekiah's mood changes (37:3 asks only for prayer; 21:2 asks for a wonder).

settings.what: A word to the house of David
settings.to: The royal family and officials who ran Judah's courts, and the people of Jerusalem who trusted their city's rock
settings.when: Not dated. It may come from Jehoiakim's reign or from Zedekiah's, and was placed here as an introduction to the sayings on the kings
settings.why: The command to judge justly "each morning" is the king's first duty (Psalm 101:8). The oracle warns that a city that trusts its walls will burn, and sets the royal house's justice as the test.
views: Scholars who read the poem as originally unconnected to the siege date it to Jehoiakim (Holladay) or leave it undated (Bright). The Greek names the valley "Sor."

title: Three Kings, One Fall
sum: Jeremiah is sent down to the king's house with a plain offer: carry out justice, protect the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, spill no innocent blood, and kings will keep entering David's gates; refuse, and the palace will become a ruin (22:1-9). Then come three kings. Josiah's son Shallum is already gone to Egypt and will not return (22:10-12). Jehoiakim built himself a cedar palace by unpaid labor, and Jeremiah sets him beside his father Josiah, who "took up the case of the poor," and asks, "Is this not knowing me?" (22:13-19). Jehoiachin, here called Coniah, will be torn off like a signet ring and thrown into a foreign land (22:24-30).

A short poem to Lebanon, Bashan and Abarim (22:20-23) pictures a proud city, nested in her cedars, with her allies broken. The chapter closes with the oracle that no descendant of Jehoiachin will sit on David's throne and rule in Judah (22:30), a verse with a long history in Jewish and Christian argument.

views.H: The kings are Josiah's sons Shallum (Jehoahaz, 609 BC), Jehoiakim (609-598) and Josiah's grandson Coniah (Jehoiachin, 598-597). Kings and Chronicles tell their stories (2 Kings 23:30-24:17). Jeremiah's words about Shallum and Coniah were borne out: Shallum died in Egypt (2 Kings 23:34), and Coniah was never allowed to return to Judah (he was released from prison in Babylon in 561 BC, 2 Kings 25:27-30, but where he died is not recorded). The oracle on Jehoiakim's burial is harder to match with the other sources (22:19 note).
views.C: The poems on Jehoiakim (22:13-19) are widely accepted as Jeremiah's own, probably from soon after 609. The prose frames (22:1-9, 22:10-12 and some of 22:24-30) are Deuteronomistic in style in the view of Thiel and Nicholson. The Greek shortens or alters 22:15, 22:18, 22:30. Verse 30 is a short prose saying with its own history of interpretation.
views.J: Jewish tradition took 22:30 seriously and answered it: Radak reasons that Jeconiah repented in captivity and so the sentence was lifted, and he points to Zerubbabel as proof (Radak on 22:30).
views.X: Matthew lists Jeconiah in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:11-12), and Christian readers have had to say how Jesus can be Davidic king through a line Jeremiah 22:30 seems to bar. The main answers: Jesus' kingship comes from God, not from a father's line; Joseph's legal fatherhood; Luke's genealogy; the reversal in Haggai 2:23 (see the deep section).
views.F: Some evangelical and dispensationalist writers argue that Jesus' claim to the throne comes through Mary's line (Luke 3), not Joseph's. Other futurist readers see the restoration of David's throne in the thousand-year reign (see 23:5-6).

deep.h: The curse on Jeconiah and Matthew 1
deep.b:
The Hebrew says that Jehoiachin will be put on record as 'ariri ("stripped of children"), and that none of his offspring will "prosper" as one who sits on David's throne and rules again in Judah (the Hebrew has a participle, "sitting," and the Plain keeps it). The first part cannot mean he had no children: 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 names seven sons, and Babylonian ration tablets list five of them. The second part is a statement about the throne, and it came true: the next king, Zedekiah, was his uncle, and no descendant of his ever ruled as king in Judah.

The difficulty is Matthew 1:11-12, where the line from David to Jesus passes through Jeconiah, Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. Four answers have been given. (1) Jesus was not Joseph's biological son. The curse falls on Jeconiah's bloodline, but Jesus' legal descent comes through Joseph (Matthew 1:16, 20-25) while his biological descent comes through Mary and David's son Nathan (Luke 3:31). (2) The curse was conditional and ended: Haggai 2:23 takes Jeconiah's grandson Zerubbabel and makes him the LORD's "signet ring," reversing the image of Jeremiah 22:24. (3) Matthew's list is built to show Jesus coming through the exile (Matthew 1:17), not to claim that the curse is void. (4) The curse concerned reigning "in Judah" as a dynasty, and Jesus' kingdom is not that. The Jewish objection is that kingship passes through the father's line, so a messiah cannot descend from Jeconiah and still be heir of David through his mother; and, in the medieval commentary of Radak, that the sentence was lifted when Jeconiah repented in captivity. A reader can weigh these without ranking them: they rest on different judgments about what the oracle meant, and about what the Gospels intend.

Jeremiah's poem on Jehoiakim sets two kings side by side. The son has a big house, fine cedar and red paint, and pays no wages. The father Josiah had food and drink as well, and "carried out justice and righteousness" (22:15); he took up the case of the poor, "and then all was well." The poem's turning point is the question "Is this not knowing me?" (22:16). For Jeremiah and his contemporary Hosea, to know the LORD is to practice justice, not only to hold a belief about him (Hosea 4:1-2; Hosea 6:6). The question is asked of a king, but it applies to anyone with power.

echoes: Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 24:17; Deuteronomy 29:24-26; 2 Kings 23:29-24:17; 2 Chronicles 36:1-10; Hosea 4:1-2; Hosea 8:8; Haggai 2:23; Matthew 1:11-12; Luke 3:31; Sirach 49:11

settings.what: Do justice, or the palace becomes a ruin
settings.by: Jeremiah, told by the LORD to go and speak
settings.to: The king of Judah, his servants and the people coming through the palace gates. No king is named
settings.when: Not dated; set in Josiah's sons' reigns, before the fall
settings.why: The speech offers the royal house the same covenant terms it had from the start: justice for the weak means the Davidic line continues; refusal means ruin by the LORD's own oath. It is the first of a series of sayings on the kings.
settings.readers: Exiles hearing it after 586 would see that the fall had been announced on conditions that were refused, and the nations' question in 22:8-9 gave them the answer to their own.

settings.what: Weep for the one who goes
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem mourning Josiah, killed at Megiddo in 609 BC, and the news that his son Shallum had been taken to Egypt
settings.when: Early in 609 BC, after Pharaoh Neco deposed Shallum (Jehoahaz) after three months
settings.why: To turn the people's grief from the dead king, whose death is over, to the exile who will never come back. Hearers who had hoped Josiah's line would continue learn it will not.

settings.to: Jehoiakim and the court that built with him, and the people who paid for it
settings.when: During Jehoiakim's reign (609-598 BC), probably after he began his palace, perhaps about 605 BC
settings.why: Jeremiah measures Jehoiakim by his father's example. The poem declares that building a showy house at the cost of the poor is the opposite of knowing the LORD, and it announces a dishonorable burial.
views: How the burial threat was fulfilled is uncertain (see the note on 22:19).

settings.by: The LORD to Jerusalem, who is a woman ("you who live in Lebanon")
settings.to: Jerusalem and her ruling class, whose allies are about to fail
settings.when: Undated; commonly placed after Jehoiakim's tribute to Babylon or after 597 BC
settings.why: The poem calls the city to mourn from the borders for the allies she had trusted. It gives the reason in 22:21: she refused to listen when she felt safe, and so now her allies are gone and no one can rescue her.

settings.to: Coniah (Jehoiachin) and his mother, and Judah ("Land, land, land")
settings.when: Spoken either in the three months of Jehoiachin's reign (December 598 to March 597 BC) or just after the deportation of 597, when verse 28 asks why he "has been flung out"
settings.why: To declare that the king's reign is over: he will be given to those he fears, die in Babylon and leave no ruling heir. Knowing that Haggai 2:23 reverses the signet-ring image, the oracle is a judgment on one man, not the end of the promise to David.
settings.readers: Readers in Babylon saw Jehoiachin in captivity and later released (52:31-34). Readers of Matthew read it again in light of Jesus' descent.
views: Many scholars place the speech after the surrender, since the verbs in 22:28 can be read as past (the Hebrew perfect can also describe a certain future, so the point is debated). Others hold it was spoken during his three-month reign, as a warning.

title: Shepherds, the Branch and the False Prophets
sum: The chapter opens by turning from kings to shepherds: Judah's rulers have scattered the flock, so the LORD will gather what is left from every land, raise up shepherds who care for them, and "raise up for David a righteous Branch," a king who will carry out justice and righteousness (23:1-6). His name will be "The LORD is our righteousness," a pointed answer to the last king, Zedekiah, whose name means "my righteousness is the LORD." The days are coming, the LORD says, when people will swear by the second Exodus, the return from the north, rather than the first (23:7-8).

Verses 9-40 turn on the prophets. Jeremiah's own heart breaks over them (23:9). Samaria's prophets spoke by Baal, but Jerusalem's, who speak in the LORD's name and promise peace, are called worse: they are like Sodom (23:13-15). They claim dreams but have not stood in the LORD's council (23:18-22). The LORD fills heaven and earth and sees them (23:23-24); his word is a fire and a hammer, and theirs is straw (23:28-29). The chapter ends with a long play on one word, massa', "oracle" and "load": the people mock Jeremiah by asking for "the oracle of the LORD," and the LORD answers that they are the load he will throw off (23:33-40).
readings: Read as the end of the monarchy and the start of a hope

The first eight verses close the collection on the kings. After the failures of Josiah's sons, the Branch is the answer: God, not a lineage, will produce the king. In this reading the promise is a response to Zedekiah in 597-586.

Jewish and Christian tradition has read the Branch as the Messiah (the Targum: a Messiah of the righteous; Radak: the Branch is the Messiah). The Church read Jesus; Jewish readers expect a king of David's line at the end of days. Neither reading needs to deny that the verse first spoke to Zedekiah's day.
Read as a warning about religious speech

The second half of the chapter is about the abuse of the LORD's name. It tests prophets by their source, their message and their effect on the people, and has been used in every century for judging preachers.

views.H: Verses 1-8 answer the failed kings of chapters 21-22 with the promise of a new shepherd. The prophets of 23:9-40 are those against whom Jeremiah argues in chapters 27-29, such as Hananiah in the temple. The whole chapter belongs to Jehoiakim's or Zedekiah's reign, and the poem on the prophets may be early.
views.C: The Greek lacks 23:30-31 and part of 23:36, reads "Josedek" for the name in 23:6, and in 23:33 reads "You are the burden." Several scholars see 23:1-8 as an editorial frame for the royal collection, with 23:5-6 an old oracle against Zedekiah that later became a messianic hope. The verses on the "oracle" (23:33-40) read as a later expansion on the word. 23:7-8 is also found at 16:14-15; its original place is debated.
views.J: Rashi explains 23:6 as "The LORD will vindicate us in this one's days"; Radak identifies the Branch with the Messiah and reads 23:7-8 as the ingathering at the end of days. The Talmud takes the hammer of 23:29 as a picture of Scripture's many meanings (Sanhedrin 34a).
views.X: Luke 1:78 uses the Greek word for the Branch, anatole (dawn), of Jesus. Paul says Christ became "our righteousness" (1 Corinthians 1:30). Christian commentators have often applied the chapter to false teachers in the church (2 Peter 2:1). The Reformation reading of "the LORD our righteousness" is the subject of the card below.
views.F: Dispensationalists and premillennialists see 23:5-8 as promising the return of Israel and the rule of the Messiah in the land in a future thousand-year kingdom; amillennial readers see it fulfilled in Christ's reign and the church; many Jews expect a messianic age in the land. The shepherds-and-sheep language leads into Ezekiel 34.

deep.h: How to tell a true prophet
deep.b: Chapter 23 puts several tests side by side. The source: the false prophets speak "a vision from their own hearts, not from the mouth of the LORD" (23:16), while a true one has "taken a stand in the council of the LORD" (23:18). The message: they say "You will have peace" to people who are doing wrong (23:17), while a true prophet would have "turned them back from their evil way" (23:22). The effect: they "put strength into the hands of evildoers" (23:14) and "bring this people no benefit at all" (23:32). The fulfillment test of Deuteronomy 18:22 is not stated here but is applied in chapters 27-28 to Hananiah. Dreams are not ruled out: the one who has a dream may tell it (23:28). The fault is calling one's own dream "the word of the LORD."

deep.h: The play on massa': oracle and load
deep.b:
The Hebrew word massa' comes from nasa', "lift." It labels a prophetic "lifting up" of the voice, an oracle (Isaiah 13:1). It is also the ordinary word for a load carried on an animal's back (2 Kings 5:17). When people mockingly ask Jeremiah, "What is the massa' of the LORD?", they treat his oracles as a heavy load. The LORD's reply uses the second sense: "What oracle? I will throw you off," or, in the reading of the Greek and Rashi, "You are the burden." Then the prophets and priests are told to stop using the word, because the "oracle" would be each man's own word, his own load. The play ends with the verb nasa' and its near-twin nashah in 23:39: "I will utterly forget you" (or "lift you up").

English cannot carry the word both ways. The KJV chose "burden" and the Plain, following this book's term list, chooses "oracle," with the other sense in the notes. The KJV's choice hides the "lifting up" of the voice; the Plain's hides the weight. The wordplay is a good example of why no single English word will do.

The new king is to be called YHWH tsidqenu. The last king was called Zedekiah, tsidqiyyahu, "my righteousness is the LORD," a name Nebuchadnezzar gave him in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:17). The two names use the same words in a different order. Zedekiah wore the name and failed to live up to it; the future king will be what the name says. Jeremiah 33:15-16 gives the same promise again, with "she" (Jerusalem) bearing the name, a difference that Jewish and Christian readers have explained in different ways. Other differences in the Hebrew: 23:5 "raise up ... a righteous Branch" against 33:15 "make ... sprout a Branch of righteousness"; 23:6 "Judah ... and Israel" against 33:16 "Judah ... and Jerusalem." The wording that is the same in Hebrew ("carry out justice and righteousness in the land"; "settle in security") should read the same in 33:15-16. In the Greek, the name is rendered as a personal name (Josedek), and the Greek lacks chapter 33:14-26 altogether.

echoes: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 18:22-33; Deuteronomy 13:1-5; Deuteronomy 18:20-22; Isaiah 11:1; Ezekiel 34:1-24; Hosea 2:16-17; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; Luke 1:78; John 10:11; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Hebrews 4:12

traditions.q: How does "The LORD is our righteousness" (23:6) make sinners right with God, and what does the title say about the one who bears it?
views: Justification is not only forgiveness but an inward renewal. The Council of Trent teaches that the only formal cause of justification is God's righteousness, not the righteousness by which God himself is just but the one by which he makes people just, so that a person is made righteous in fact and not only reckoned righteous (Session 6, chapter 7). The Catechism speaks of justification as conforming a person to the righteousness of God, who makes them inwardly just (paragraph 1992). Catholic readers hear the title as saying that the righteousness is the LORD's gift, which makes the believer just and does not only count him so; the Catechism and Trent state this doctrine in general terms.

Christ's righteousness is counted as the believer's own, by faith alone. The Formula of Concord rejects the view of Andreas Osiander, who used this text to teach that Christ's divine nature dwelling in believers is their righteousness. Epitome III answers that the whole Christ, God and man, is our righteousness, citing Jeremiah 23:6 with 1 Corinthians 1:30 (as reported in Lutheran commentary on the Epitome), and that what makes the sinner righteous before God is Christ's obedience counted as his own, with new obedience following as fruit.

Righteousness is imputed. Calvin answers Osiander in the Institutes (3.11) and teaches that Christ is our righteousness as his obedience is credited to believers; in his Jeremiah commentary on this verse he argues the grammar (whether the LORD is the one who names or the one named) and not only imputation, and the Westminster Confession says God justifies by "imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ" to them (chapter 11).

Baptist confessions teach the Reformed answer in their own words: God justifies sinners by "imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ" to them, received by faith alone (Second London Confession, chapter 11). Baptists who preach on this verse read the name as pointing to Christ as the believer's righteousness.

John Wesley preached a sermon on this text, "The Lord Our Righteousness" (1765). He holds that Christ's righteousness is imputed to believers for pardon, and also insists that an inward holiness must follow, since the same Lord who is our righteousness also makes us righteous.
Article 11 says we are "accounted righteous before God" only for the merit of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ by faith, not for our own works; the Church's homilies add that good works follow.

Orthodox teaching does not describe salvation mainly as a legal verdict. It speaks of healing and of sharing in the life of God (theosis), and does not separate being declared righteous from being made holy. On this reading, "the LORD is our righteousness" says that the LORD himself is given to the believer, not a credited status. The Orthodox Church has no official statement on this verse; the frame is described by Ware and Lossky.

settings.what: Shepherds who scatter, a Branch who rules
settings.to: The rulers of Judah (the shepherds), and the scattered people addressed in the second half as the flock
settings.when: Undated. One view, followed here, places the oracle in Zedekiah's reign after 597 BC as an answer to him; another holds that 23:1-8 was gathered for the book after 586 BC. Either way it was placed after the sayings on the kings
settings.why: To close the royal collection with a verdict and a promise. The kings who lost the flock will be called to account, and the LORD will gather the flock and give it a king who does what Jehoiakim and Zedekiah did not. The new name answers Zedekiah's.
settings.readers: Exiles in Babylon read 23:3-4 and 23:7-8 as a promise of return from "all the lands"; the later church and synagogue read 23:5-6 as the hope for the Messiah.
views: Some scholars place the oracle during Zedekiah's reign, as a counter-name to his. Others place it after 586, when the dynasty had ended, and see it as a reply to the loss of the throne.

settings.to: The prophets and priests of Jerusalem and the people who listened to them
settings.when: Not dated; the arguments match those of chapters 27-29 in Zedekiah's reign, but some of the poems may come from Jehoiakim's time
settings.why: To tell the people not to trust prophets who promise peace. Their sin is not wrong doctrine alone but reaching the people with their own words under the LORD's name, so that no one repents. The speech tells the hearers how to test what they hear.
settings.readers: For exiles and later readers, who had no prophet at hand, the chapter explained why so many had been wrong before 586 and gave a test for later prophets.

settings.what: "What is the oracle of the LORD?"
settings.to: The people, prophets and priests who ask Jeremiah for "the oracle of the LORD," and the prophet himself
settings.when: Not dated; likely addressed in Jerusalem before 586
settings.why: To stop the casual use of the formula "oracle of the LORD" in mockery or in false prophecy. People may ask what the LORD has answered, but they may not label their own words with his name.

title: Two Baskets of Figs
sum: After Jeconiah and Judah's leading men have been taken to Babylon, the LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple: one of very good, early figs; the other of figs so bad they cannot be eaten (24:1-3). The good figs are the exiles of 597 BC. The LORD will look on them for good, bring them back, build them up and plant them, and give them a heart to know him (24:5-7). The bad figs are Zedekiah, his officials, the people left in the land and those who live in Egypt, who will become a horror and a byword among all the nations until the sword, famine and disease finish them (24:8-10).
The vision turns the people's own view upside down. Those left in Jerusalem thought they were safe and the exiles were cast out. The LORD says the reverse.

views.H: The vision belongs to the early years of Zedekiah (597-586 BC), after the first deportation. The deportees included Jehoiachin, the court, the craftsmen and smiths (2 Kings 24:14-16). Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (chapter 29) and his later warning about Egypt (chapters 42-44) are the same message in prose.
views.C: Many critics (Carroll, among others) see the chapter as shaped by the Babylonian exiles' claim to be the true Israel and the others as the rejected; Thiel and Nicholson see Deuteronomistic wording in verses 5-10. The Greek reads "the Jews who were carried away" in 24:5, lists "the craftsmen, the prisoners and the neighbors" in 24:1, and has a different list of shames in 24:9, but lacks nothing large. 4QJer-c has parts of 24:6-7 (several words restored) and agrees with the Masoretic Text in the words that survive.
views.J: Jewish tradition read 24 with 29 as a consolation to the exiles. The good figs stand for the community that kept Israel's identity in Babylon, which became the center of Jewish learning for a thousand years.
views.X: Christians have read the vision as a lesson that outward status does not decide God's favor, and have seen in the new heart (24:7) a first form of the new covenant (31:33). The picture of fruit judged by quality echoes Jesus' sayings about good and bad fruit and the fig tree (Matthew 7:16-20; Luke 13:6-9).
views.F: Futurist readers see little here beyond the return after the seventy years; some apply 24:6-7 to the final regathering of Israel.

deep.h: Whose land? The good and the bad figs
deep.b:
After 597 BC two groups claimed to be Israel. In Jerusalem, the people left behind took the exiles' departure as proof that God had cast them out and given the land to those who stayed (Ezekiel 11:15). In Babylon, the exiles hoped for a quick return (29:8). Jeremiah's vision answers both: the exiles are not the discard but the good figs, and there is no safety in Jerusalem. It does not claim that every exile is righteous (see the false prophets among them, 29:21-23). The figs are two destinies, not a list of individuals.

The vision also sets out the book's call-verbs in reverse order for the exiles ("build" and "plant," not "tear down" and "uproot"), and gives the grounds of their restoration in verse 7: not their merit but a new heart given by the LORD. This is the book's usual pattern: God both asks for return and enables it (31:18).

echoes: Deuteronomy 26:1-4; Amos 8:1-2; Hosea 9:10; Ezekiel 11:15-20; Matthew 7:16-20; Luke 13:6-9; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3

settings.what: The vision of the two baskets of figs
settings.by: The LORD, showing Jeremiah a vision and explaining it
settings.to: Jeremiah first; then Judah under Zedekiah, both those still in Jerusalem and those in Egypt, and the exiles in Babylon
settings.when: After the deportation of Jehoiachin and the court in 597 BC, and before the fall of Jerusalem in 586
settings.why: To correct what the survivors in Jerusalem believed: that they were the favored remnant and the exiles the rejected. The vision gives the exiles hope for return and warns Zedekiah's circle that there is no refuge in the land or in Egypt.
settings.readers: For the exiles reading the book, it said that their suffering was not rejection. For those who had stayed, and for refugees in Egypt, it was a warning.
views: Traditional readers hear Jeremiah's own comfort to the exiles. Many critical scholars hear the exiles' later claim to be the true community, expressed in Jeremiah's name (Carroll).

title: Seventy Years and the Cup
sum: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605-604 BC), the year Nebuchadnezzar became king, Jeremiah reviews twenty-three years of warning, from Josiah's thirteenth year, and says the people never listened (25:1-7). Because of that, the LORD will send for the clans of the north and for Nebuchadnezzar "my servant." The land will become a ruin, all joy will stop, the nations will serve Babylon seventy years, and then Babylon itself will be punished (25:8-14).

The second half is the cup of the wine of the LORD's rage. Jeremiah is told to make every nation drink it, from Jerusalem first, then Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, Sidon, the Arabian tribes, Elam, Media, the kings of the north, and last of all the king of "Sheshach," a cipher for Babylon (25:15-29). The LORD roars from on high like a lion, a shout like grape treaders, and the shepherds of the nations are told to howl (25:30-38). In the Greek Bible the oracles against the nations come right after verse 13, and the cup passage is moved to chapter 32.
readings: Read as the turning point of the book

Chapter 25 sums up the first half (twenty-three years of unheeded warnings), announces Babylon's coming, and gives the span of its power. It opens the oracles against the nations, which in the Greek follow here.
Critical scholars read it as an edited speech, with Deuteronomistic wording in 25:3-7 and a later layer in 25:11-14, summing up the book rather than a speech of 605 BC as it stands.

views.H: The fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605-604 BC, is the year of Carchemish and of Nebuchadnezzar's accession; the Babylonian Chronicle records Babylon's control of the whole region ("Hatti") the following year. The "clans of the north" are Babylon and its allies; the "seventy years" run from Babylon's rise to its fall, or from the temple's fall to its rebuilding (see the note on 25:11). The cup list reads as a map of the region in the early 6th century.
views.C: The Greek and Hebrew differ widely: the Greek omits Nebuchadnezzar's name at 25:9, "king of Babylon" at 25:11-12, verse 14, Sheshach, and several nations; it puts the oracles against the nations here and moves the cup passage to chapter 32. Tov and Bogaert read this as evidence for an earlier, shorter Hebrew edition; others hold the Greek abbreviated. 4QJer-c has parts of 25:7-8, 25:15-17 and 25:24-26, but most of its words in 25:24-25 are restored. Its visible words show the long text at 25:7 (the end of the verse, in part), at "Zimri" in 25:25 and at the king of Sheshach in 25:26.
views.J: The seventy years became the key number in Jewish reckoning of the exile; Daniel 9 reads them again as seventy weeks of years. Rashi reads "Sheshach" as Babylon in atbash. The cup of wrath is a recurring image of divine judgment on the nations in Isaiah 51 and Psalm 75.
views.X: Revelation takes the cup of wrath (Revelation 14:10; 16:19) and Babylon's fall (Revelation 18:22-23 uses Jeremiah 25:10), and the New Testament reads Jesus' Gethsemane prayer in light of the cup (Matthew 26:39). Many Christian writers have used the seventy years to date the return and Daniel's seventy weeks to date the Messiah.
views.F: Futurist readers who take the seventy years as fulfilled in the return under Cyrus point to a future cup of wrath on the nations in the great tribulation; they read Revelation 14-18 as its fulfilment. Others read the cup as a recurring pattern of judgment.

deep.b: Jeremiah gives the number twice, 25:11-12 and 29:10, and Daniel 9:2 says he understood it from "the books." Four ways of counting are in use. Babylon's era: from 605 BC (Nebuchadnezzar's rise) to 539 (Cyrus takes Babylon), about 66 years, rounded up; this fits "these nations will serve the king of Babylon." Temple to temple: from the burning of the temple in 586 to its rebuilding in 516 BC, exactly seventy, as Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5 count. The land's sabbath: Chronicles reads the seventy years as the rest owed to the land for the sabbath years Israel had not kept (2 Chronicles 36:21; Leviticus 26:34-35). A round number: seventy is a lifetime (Psalm 90:10) and a conventional length of divine anger; an inscription of Esarhaddon says the god Marduk planned seventy years of desolation for Babylon, then relented and made them eleven, and Isaiah 23:15 gives Tyre seventy years. Daniel 9:24 reinterprets them as seventy weeks of years, 490, a reading Jews and Christians have used for different ends. Any of these can be right for different verses: the span for the nations' service to Babylon need not be the span of the exiles' stay.
deep.refs: 25:11-12; 29:10; 2 Chronicles 36:21; Daniel 9:2; Daniel 9:24; Zechariah 1:12; Zechariah 7:5; Isaiah 23:15

deep.b: In the Hebrew Bible Jeremiah 25:13 ends with "which Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations," and chapters 26-45 follow, with the oracles against the nations in 46-51. In the Greek the oracles against the nations follow 25:13 directly (Greek 25:14-31:44, Swete's numbering), beginning with Elam, and the clause "what Jeremiah prophesied against the nations" stands there as their heading, without "all"; the cup passage of Hebrew 25:15-38 comes after them as Greek chapter 32, and the Greek then continues with the temple sermon trial (Hebrew 26). Pierre-Maurice Bogaert and Emanuel Tov argue that the Greek's order is the older one, and that the Hebrew moved the nations' oracles to the end, adding material as it went. Others argue the Greek translator rearranged. The Dead Sea Scrolls show that both short and long Hebrew texts circulated (4QJer-b and -d are short; 4QJer-a, -c and -e are long), which suggests the shorter text was not just the translator's work.

The cup list ends with "the king of Sheshach." The name exists nowhere else, but in the letter-swap code called atbash it spells Babel. Jeremiah uses the same device at 51:41, and "Leb-qamai" in 51:1 is atbash for "Chaldeans." Rashi says plainly that Sheshach is Babylon in atbash. The point of the code is debated: a hint of caution while Babylon was in power, a scribal play, or a later editor's addition. The Greek lacks the sentence, but 4QJer-c has it. The placing is sharp in any case: Babylon comes last in the list of nations that drink. Separately, 51:7 pictures Babylon as a golden cup in the LORD's hand that made the whole earth drunk.

echoes: Leviticus 26:34-35; 2 Chronicles 36:21-23; Isaiah 51:17-22; Psalm 75:8; Habakkuk 2:15-16; Amos 1:2; Ezekiel 9:6; Daniel 9:2; Zechariah 1:12; Matthew 26:39; 1 Peter 4:17; Revelation 14:10; Revelation 18:22-23

settings.what: Twenty-three years of warning, and seventy years of Babylon
settings.to: All the people of Judah and everyone living in Jerusalem
settings.when: The fourth year of Jehoiakim, the first of Nebuchadnezzar (605-604 BC), the year Jeremiah's first scroll was dictated (36:1)
settings.why: To tell the nation what its twenty-three years of refusal had cost: the LORD would use Babylon, and the land and its neighbors would serve Babylon for seventy years before Babylon's own turn. Knowing the date makes the passage a warning at the moment Babylon became the region's master, not an account after the fall.
settings.readers: To the exiles and later readers, the chapter fixed the length of the exile and the promise that Babylon would be judged in its time; it also gave them the reason for it.
views: The date is widely accepted as accurate, but many scholars hold the prose as shaped by later editors, with 25:11-14 added after 539 BC. Others hold it comes from Jeremiah or Baruch.

settings.what: The cup of the wine of rage
settings.by: Jeremiah, reporting a command from the LORD and what he did
settings.to: The nations on the list, with Judah and Jerusalem first; the Judeans who heard the report
settings.when: Dated by its place to the same moment (605-604 BC), though the list may have been shaped later
settings.why: To show that the LORD's judgment is not on Judah alone: every nation, including Babylon last, drinks. For Judah it removes the idea that the LORD's name protects them: they drink first.
views: Whether Jeremiah literally gave the cup, saw it in a vision, or delivered it in words is debated (see the note on 25:17).

settings.what: The LORD roars against the earth
settings.by: The LORD, told to Jeremiah to prophesy
settings.to: All who live on the earth, and in practice the people of Judah and the rulers of the nations (the shepherds)
settings.when: As part of the same speech, though some take the poem as a separate piece placed here
settings.why: To show the cup in action: God as a lion, a winepress and a storm, with the rulers unable to escape. For Judah's hearers, the poem showed that judgment would reach the leaders everywhere.
